title: Bank Governance, Regulation, and Risk Taking
research_question: Does the ownership structure of a bank shape its risk-taking behavior, and does the effect of national bank regulations—such as capital requirements, deposit insurance, and restrictions on bank activities—on bank risk depend on the comparative power of shareholders within each bank's governance structure? Additionally, how do shareholder protection laws moderate the relationship between concentrated ownership and bank risk?
data_description: The authors compile a new bank-level dataset covering up to 296 of the largest publicly listed banks (by total assets at end-2001) across 48 countries, with on average more than 80% of national banking system assets represented. Bank ownership data, drawn from Caprio et al. (2007) and supplemented by hand-collection from Bankers Almanac, Bankscope, 20-F filings, annual reports, and company websites, include direct and indirect voting and cash-flow rights of the largest owner, managerial ownership, board composition, and founder involvement. Accounting data come from Bankscope and equity returns from Datastream. Risk is measured by the bank's z-score (1996–2001), volatility of weekly equity returns (1999–2001), and earnings volatility (1996–2001). Country-level variables include shareholder rights (La Porta et al. 1998), capital regulation, activity restrictions, and deposit insurance indicators (Barth et al. 2006; Demirguc-Kunt et al. 2008), GDP per capita, concentration, enforcement, and M&A activity.
institutional_context: Banks operate under widely varying national regulatory regimes—covering capital adequacy requirements, explicit or implicit deposit insurance, and restrictions on engaging in securities, insurance, real estate, and nonfinancial firm ownership—as well as under heterogeneous shareholder protection laws. At the same time, banks differ enormously in ownership structure: in some countries (e.g., Canada, Ireland, the United States) the largest banks are predominantly widely held, while in 22 of 48 sample countries no large bank is widely held and controlling shareholders—families, corporations, or the state—hold substantial cash-flow and voting rights, sometimes through pyramidal chains. Classic agency tensions arise because diversified equity owners with limited liability favor greater risk-taking, whereas non-shareholder managers with bank-specific human capital and private control benefits prefer prudence. This combination of cross-country regulatory diversity and within-country variation in controlling-shareholder power motivates examining how regulation and governance jointly shape bank risk.
